## Registrations {#every-reanalysis-leaves-a-public-trail}

::: {.small}
- A registration is "a frozen version of your project that can never be edited or deleted, but you can issue a withdrawal of it later"
- It is time-stamped, with an identifier of its own, a DOI once public, and an embargo of up to four years if needed
- For new data, it fixes the plan before the data are collected; for a reanalysis, before the analytical choices are made
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The replication of the housing-audit claim uploaded its preregistration on 5 May 2020, registered it on 14 May 2020 under an embargo until 13 May 2024 (osf.io/v6wd8), and uploaded its final report on 7 October 2020, so the plan came first.
:::

::: {.src}
The help pages of the OSF on registrations; the SCORE project of the housing-audit paper, osf.io/3a8bg.
:::

::: notes
A registration is what the OSF calls a frozen document. In the words of its help pages, it is a frozen version of your project that can never be edited or deleted, though you can withdraw it later. It carries a timestamp and an identifier, gets a DOI once it is public, and can stay private under an embargo of up to four years. That is the mechanism behind preregistration. For new data it records the plan before the data are collected, and for a reanalysis, before the specific choices are made. [advance] Here is one that did its job, in the housing-audit case: the replication registered its plan in May 2020, kept it under embargo while the work ran, and reported in October. Because the plan is dated before the report, nobody can say that the analysis was chosen to fit the result.
:::

## The Multi100 preregistration {#the-study-you-are-inside-was-preregistered}

::: {.small}
- Multi100 was preregistered on the OSF after its analysts had been recruited and before any analysis began
- The registration fixed the aim, the two questions and the rule for comparing effect sizes: a new result counts as different when it lies beyond ±0.05 Cohen's *d* of the original
- A second preregistration covered the peer evaluation of the reanalyses
- The outcome: 74% of the reanalyses reached the same conclusion, and 34% came within ±0.05 *d*
:::

::: {.src}
Preregistrations osf.io/4ev9t (pp. 2 and 9) and osf.io/y4evp; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness [p. 136].
:::

::: notes
Multi100 practised what it measured. Its first preregistration was filed after the analysts had been recruited and before any of them had started, and it fixed the questions and, above all, the judging: two results count as the same when their effect sizes lie within five hundredths of a Cohen's d. It even explains why it sets confidence intervals aside, since a less precise estimate would look more robust. A second registration covered the peer evaluation. That is why the seventy-four per cent and the thirty-four per cent of the last session mean something, because nobody could move the goalposts once the results were in. The course repeats this design on the second day, with you as a sixth analyst who declares an analysis before running it.
:::

## Preregistration templates {#two-templates-one-choice}

::: {.small}
- **The AsPredicted form**, on the OSF as the "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org": eight short questions, from whether any data have been collected to the sample size. The preregistration block of the course follows it, adapted for data already in hand
- **The template for secondary data**: 25 questions, written for the analysis of existing data, among them questions on what you already know about the data and their results [@VandenAkkerEtAl2021PreregistrationSecondaryData, p. 3]
- Both are set out in the reading of this session
:::

::: notes
Two templates matter for a reanalysis. The AsPredicted form asks eight questions in plain language, and the preregistration block of the course follows it. But it was written for people who have not collected their data yet, and its first question, whether any data have been collected, has for us the awkward answer that we already hold everything. The template that van den Akker and colleagues wrote for secondary data is built for exactly that situation: twenty-five questions, among them a set on what you already know about the data and how you came to know it. A preregistration of a reanalysis cannot promise that you approached the data blind, only that your choices were fixed and dated before you ran them, and the block of the course borrows that part as its data-in-hand statement.
:::
